summary: Defines additional MIB objects for managing ADSL interfaces that were not covered by the ADSL Line MIB in RFC 2662, extending the ability to monitor and configure these digital subscriber lines.

eli5.summary: ADSL lines are the wires that bring Internet to many homes. This note adds more meters and switches so operators can watch and control them.

questions: what is the adsl line extension mib
subtitle: Extra SNMP objects for ADSL lines: transmission modes, G.Lite power states, more error counters and alarm thresholds.

tldr.problem: The ADSL Line MIB (RFC 2662) does not cover some objects defined in ITU G.997.1, such as the transmission mode in use, G.Lite power state and fast retrain counts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3440 defines a supplementary MIB module, ADSL-LINE-EXT-MIB, that augments the RFC 2662 tables with transmission mode objects, extra counters, a dual-mode profile, a line type setting and threshold notifications.
tldr.outcome: It lets a manager see and configure the ADSL line mode, power state, retrains, severely errored seconds and unavailable seconds. It is a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFC in the metadata.

today: RFC 3440 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It supplements the ADSL Line MIB in RFC 2662.

sections.title: Purpose and Framework
sections.content:
RFC 3440 defines a supplemental set of managed objects that the ADSL Line MIB (RFC 2662) does not cover. It addresses additional objects defined in ITU G.997.1. The module is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580) and, like other MIBs, is normally accessed with SNMP; the overall framework is described in RFC 3410.

The MIB follows the same structure as the ADSL Line MIB. Its new tables use AUGMENTS, so each new entry extends an existing RFC 2662 entry for the same line.
sections.eli5: An earlier note made a set of meters for ADSL lines. This one adds a few more that were missing.

sections.title: Interface Status and Power States
sections.content:
The ADSL Line Extension MIB follows the conventions of the ADSL Line MIB with one exception. The ifOperStatus object from RFC 2863 SHALL be down(2) when the ADSL line interface is in power state L3, which means no power. It is up(1) in state L0 (power on) or L1 (reduced power). Power state L2 is not applicable.

For lines in G.Lite mode, there are three power states: L0 power on, L1 power on but reduced, and L3 power off. An operator cannot configure the power state, but can view it through ifOperStatus or the new adslLineGlitePowerState object. That object reads none(1) unless the line is in a G.992.2 (G.Lite) mode.
sections.eli5: A line can be fully on, half asleep or off. You can look at which, but you cannot set it from here.

sections.title: Transmission Modes and Line Mode
sections.content:
Three objects are added to monitor and configure the ATU-C transmission system: adslLineTransAtucCap (what the equipment can do), adslLineTransAtucConfig (what is enabled, read-write) and adslLineTransAtucActual (what is in use). They use the AdslTransmissionModeType bit string, with one bit per mode, from bit 0 for ANSI T1.413 to bit 12 for G.992.1 TCM-ISDN symmetric.

Each transmission mode implies a line mode, either Full or G.Lite. If more than one bit is configured and both Full and G.Lite modes are selected, the interface is in dual mode. Only one bit can be set in the Actual object. It returns 0 if the mode is not known.
sections.eli5: An ADSL line can talk in several styles. You can ask which styles the box knows, which you allowed, and which one it is using right now.

sections.title: New Counters and Interval Tables
sections.content:
Two counters from G.997.1 section 7.4.15, the fast retrain count and the failed fast retrain count, are added to all performance tables. So are two more: severely errored seconds-line and unavailable seconds-line. Unavailable seconds do not include seconds in which unavailability was caused solely by fast retrains and failed fast retrains, which are considered part of normal network operation.

Counters follow the ADSL Line MIB pattern: totals since agent reset, a current 15-minute interval, up to 96 history buckets of 15 minutes, and current and previous 1-day values. Counters are not reset when an ATU-C or ATU-R is reinitialized, only when the agent is reset or reinitialized. The ATU-C gets all four new counters; the ATU-R gets only the two second-line counters.

An agent need not align 15-minute intervals with any wall clock, though some implementations may align them with quarter hours.
sections.eli5: The line keeps score of how many times it had to restart and how many seconds were bad, for the last quarter hour, the last day and more.

sections.title: Profiles and Alarm Thresholds
sections.content:
The object adslLineConfProfileDualLite is used only for dual mode. The existing adslLineConfProfile from RFC 2662 is the primary full-rate profile; the new object describes the G.Lite profile. With dynamic profiles it equals the index of the applicable profile row. With static profiles its value is an algorithmic name: the ifIndex plus Full or Lite, as a fixed-length string of 14 characters with leading zeros, for example 0000000015Full for ifIndex 15 on a full-rate line.

adslConfProfileLineType sets the physical line mode: no channel, fast only, interleaved only, fast or interleaved, or fast and interleaved.

Five new threshold objects, each an Integer32 from 0 to 900 seconds, control notifications for the current 15-minute bucket. The value 0, which is also the default, disables the notification. Five notifications are defined, such as adslAtucSesLThreshTrap, each sent the first time its counter reaches or exceeds the threshold in a 15-minute period.
sections.eli5: You can set alarms that ring when too many bad seconds pile up in a quarter hour. Setting an alarm to zero turns it off.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content:
Compliance is given in the MIB module itself. The ATU-C agent compliance statement makes three groups mandatory: the extended line group, the profile control group and the alarm profile group. Three more are optional: the ATU-C physical counter group, the ATU-R physical counter group and the notifications group, which implementations that support Threshold Crossing Alerts should implement.

The threshold objects may be only read-write, and the dual-mode profile object only read-only, when static profiles from RFC 2662 are implemented.
sections.eli5: The note lists which meters every device must have and which are optional extras.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that blocking unauthorized access to the ADSL MIB is outside its scope, and that access would let someone modify profiles. That could interfere with subscriber service (rate partitioning, maximum transmission rates) and with network operations (notification thresholds such as SNR margins).

SNMPv1 by itself is insecure, so implementors are encouraged to use SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415). The profile choice (static or dynamic) must be consistent with the RFC 2662 implementation. Finally, a subscriber with ADSL-layer access from the ATU-R might generate enough notifications to overwhelm the management interface or the element manager.
sections.eli5: Whoever can change these settings can mess up customers' service, so only trusted people should be allowed to use them.

items.label: fastOrInterleaved
items.desc: Either channel can exist, but only one at a time.

items.label: fastAndInterleaved
items.desc: Both the fast and the interleaved channel exist.
